Experiential Learning

Justin Pugliese MA

Justin Pugliese

16 West 10th Street
New York, NY 10011

Justin Pugliese   Social service supervisor at Women in Need, Inc.'s Stone House supportive housing residence. He is a student at CMPS.

In this paper, the author describes his experiences in the advisement orientation group that he worked in for his first two semesters as an analyst in training at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He explores how being a member of such a group, led by an experienced, expert practitioner of modern psychoanalysis, taught him about the process of learning to become a modern psychoanalyst. Topics discussed include: transference as an educational tool, emotional communications in the classroom, resistance to regression as resistance to learning, the importance of cultivating a spirit of freedom regarding the capacity to experience and express all feelings, and the relationship between fantasies about feelings and orientation to reality.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Meaning and Melancholia: Life in the Age of Bewilderment, Christopher Bollas. New York: Routledge, 2018. 142 pp.

Nancy Gerber

Nancy Gerber

Nancy Gerber  

Christopher Bollas's new book is a manifesto, a social critique, and a challenge to thinking, sentient beings. His aim is to analyze group psychologies and the psychodynamics of culture, in order to provide insight into the contemporary political climate of divisiveness and hatred. He seeks to add a discussion of societal mental health issues to the current geopolitical discourse because the denial of psychological factors at the national and international levels “is a lobotomy that imperils us all” (p. xxvii).

Bollas is interested in the ways in which psychological “axioms” constitute a mentality that defines a group and are represented in literature and other cultural forms of expression (xxi). These axioms, or patterns of belief, become “structuralized” within the mind and influence group behavior (p. xx). Internalized axioms form a kind of collective unconscious that drives the behavior of groups and nations.

Not all axioms are oppressive. In examining the cultural and political history of the West, Bollas juxtaposes the drive for war and destruction (or Thanatos, though he does not use the term) against a more libidinal striving: the quest for meaning. A collective search for meaning bound social groups together for centuries. Even those who were oppressed by poverty and social inequality identified with the ideology that life was imbued with meaning (p. xxvi).

responseSet.title: Advice Not Given: A Guide to Getting over Yourself by Mark Epstein, M.D. New York: Penguin, 2018. 204 pp.
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Advice Not Given: A Guide to Getting over Yourself by Mark Epstein, M.D. New York: Penguin, 2018. 204 pp.

George Ernsberger

George Ernsberger

George Ernsberger  

The several books of the New York psychiatrist and psychotherapist Mark Epstein are widely known, but are in none of the usual senses technical or theoretical, so they haven't been covered here. They are nevertheless well worth the attention of practitioners and patients, and this most recent one is a good place to begin a relationship with him. The central fact of his identity as a writer is that he is a Buddhist in belief and in practice, as well as a Freudian. It seems clear that he relates to his psychotherapy patients in the ways that the analytic contract intends; Buddhist beliefs and assumptions might well, or might never, enter that relationship over time as both partners in the relationship find useful. (He has said that his books prompt some prospective patients to approach him for treatment explicitly because they find that aspect of his thinking attractive.)

The man who became known as the Buddha, Epstein reminds us, was no more a god than Freud was; rather, a student, both reverent and fearless, of human nature (and of other things, as Freud was and we all are). And: these two ways of understanding and of ministering to the mind are detectably different but clearly compatible—harmonic, might be said. Crucially, both declare themselves as knowing and accepting that the minds that we humans are operating terrify us, and that much of our vital energy is spent in keeping all that's in there under control and out of sight, including, as much as possible, our own sight.

111

responseSet.title: Introduction
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Introduction

Faye Newsome

Faye Newsome

Faye Newsome  

This issue of Modern Psychoanalysis is organized around articles written by candidates in training at some of the psychoanalytic training centers where modern psychoanalytic theory is studied and taught. One of the primary goals of the educational process at these schools is to resolve resistances to learning—central among which is avoiding conscious awareness of unpleasant ideas, feelings, or reactions to the patient—either subjective or objective countertranference responses. Hyman Spotnitz (1985) characterized some of these in his Modern Psychoanalysis of the Schizophrenic Patient as the need not to feel hate, the need to be liked, and the need to be right.

These student authors each experienced one or more of those resistances, along with others. With input from instructors, supervisors, classmates, and sometimes the synergy generated in their personal training analysis, they made progress in their own development toward becoming more confident and proficient in the difficult, aspirational task of learning to have, consciously and comfortably, more of their thoughts and feelings, and how to use those in a constructive, therapeutic way with their patients.

David Rothauser   Psychoanalyst in training at CMPS. He holds master's degrees in education and psychoanalysis and is a graduate of the Center for Group Studies. David has applied psychodynamic principles in public education and currently works as an executive coach and consultant to individuals and organizations.

The author reports on the development of his understanding of and ability to use the modern psychoanalytic technique of following the patient's contact. The analyst in training traces that process in his experience at a field placement site, working with a patient with aphasia. That near-total inability to speak was, of course, a particular challenge in forming a therapeutic relationship in a treatment process that is known as the talking cure. The author examines how, early on, he misunderstood and misused the technique of following the contact. Applying ideas from attachment theory and the concept of play, he explores his development inside and outside the treatment room that enabled him to follow the patient's contact more effectively, which led to the formation of a therapeutic relationship.

The author sketches the history of the concept of transference from its earliest usages in Freud, and then reflects carefully on its inner nature, neurologically as well as psychologically, finding in the neurological research of Brockman and Fuster essential confirmation of Freud's insights and the later thinking on the subject by such modern psychoanalysts as Spotnitz, Meadow, and Margolis. responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

On Mental Growth: Bion's Ideas That Transform Psychoanalytical Clinical Practice. Lia Pistiner de Cortiñas. London: Karnac Books Ltd., 2017, 195 pp.

Paul Moore

Paul Moore

Paul Moore  

Lia Pistiner de Cortiñas looks at Bion's work with a particular emphasis on the origins of thoughts, feelings and experience. Applied to the treatment room, mental growth is about recognizing patients' difficulties in thinking or feeling their problems, not the problems themselves. Such a shift in focus is crucial because you cannot help someone with a problem that they are not able to experience. Pistiner, via Bion, notes that this capacity to “take in” experience can be impaired in early development, when desire gets overly frustrated or when pain finds no containment. What is left can be omnipotent projective identification, an underdeveloped ego that splits experience into minute particles that get ejected into experience, only to return as bizarre and persecutory objects, which once again have to be ejected. One could see these projections as fragmented psychic particles, the broken pieces of the contact barrier, looking for another person to contain them and carry them to term. Pistiner also reorients us to Bion's idea of knowing, which, when it leads to truth, stimulates emotional and psychological growth. This seems to come from Bion's (1967) idea that:

… healthy mental growth seems to depend on truth as the living organism depends on food. If it is lacking or deficient the personality deteriorates. I cannot support this conviction by evidence regarded as scientific. It may be that the formulation belongs to the domain of Aesthetic. In practice the problem arises with schizoid personalities in whom the super-ego appears to be developmentally prior to the ego and to deny development and existence itself to the ego. The usurpation by the super-ego of the position that should be occupied by the ego involves imperfect development of the reality principle, and exaltation of a “moral” outlook and lack of respect for the truth. The result is starvation of the psyche and stunted growth. (p. 38)

As Pistiner makes clear, the discovery and apprehension of knowledge is a deeply emotional experience and implies an openness and receptivity to the vicissitudes of experience. Most of all, truth is intimately intertwined with our capacity or incapacity to have an experience.
